messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mark, a 58-year-old dentist in a long-term relationship, still flinched every time a patient’s shadow fell across the operatory doorway—a reflex that had begun three years earlier, after a traffic stop turned into what he could only describe as a beating. He had been driving home from a late appointment when two officers mistook his sedan for a stolen vehicle, pulled him out, and spent several minutes on his back and ribs while he pleaded. The memory returned not as a coherent story but as pieces that belonged to someone else: the metallic crunch of a boot against his spine, the scrape of asphalt across his cheek, the officer’s voice ordering him to stay down. He knew it had happened to him, yet the scenes felt like a film he had stumbled into by mistake. That sense of dislocation was the only way his mind seemed able to hold what his body had endured.

Over the following months, Mark became convinced that some flaw in him had drawn the violence. He replayed the moment the patrol car’s lights came on and asked himself what he could have said, how he could have looked, to signal *different*—as if his own face or posture had been an invitation. This belief that his intrinsic fault was to blame made the memories feel even more alien; they belonged to a version of himself who had been weak or wrong, a person he no longer recognized. When the auditory flashbacks came—a sharp command, a crack of radio static—his ribs would ache as if freshly struck, and he would wonder whether the man in those sounds was even him.

To keep the memories at bay, Mark began steering his life into a narrow channel. He avoided anything that might stir emotion, positive or negative, because feeling anything seemed to crack the seal on the pain recall. He cancelled a dinner with old friends because the restaurant would be crowded and unpredictable. At his dental practice, he outfitted the waiting room with partitions so he could not see who was approaching the front desk, and he arranged his own operatory chair so his back faced a solid wall. He checked every new patient’s name, then scanned the hallway before leaving a room. Still, the threat of strangers felt constant: a man walking too close on the sidewalk, a delivery driver who lingered at the door—each one triggered a spike of auditory recall, the officer’s voice overlapping with the present moment, and a fresh wave of pain in his lower back.

That sense of threat also worsened his sleep. He lay awake listening for footsteps in the hall, his body braced, and when he finally drifted off, the dream version of the stop always ended with a blow he could not avoid. Waking from these nightmares, he would lie rigid and replay the injustice: no charges were filed, no apology came, the officers’ names were never released. That feeling of being crushed by an unfair system reinforced his belief that his life had been destroyed—not just physically but morally, chronologically. Every avoidance, every checking of the room, every refusal to let a stranger stand behind him at a checkout line only confirmed that he was now a person who had to live this way.

The patterns tightened into a loop he could not see. Because he avoided all stress, he never went to the small park where he used to walk; because he never walked there, he never gave himself the chance to learn that strangers on a path were not officers with badges. Because he checked his surroundings compulsively, he stayed hypervigilant, and hypervigilance kept the auditory recall present. The alien quality of the memory—the sense that the whole event had happened to a different man—meant he could not integrate it into his story, so it stayed raw and easily triggered. And each triggered memory reaffirmed that he was fundamentally marked, that the injustice was permanent, that his life was over.

What finally brought Mark to a therapist was his partner’s quiet observation that he had not touched her in months—not out of anger but because he had shut down all feeling, even affection. He came not hoping to erase the memory, but terrified that he might never again feel like the person he had been before the lights came on in his rearview mirror.
